here's the draft:

Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. While certain relatives vanished during his six months of agonizing illness only to reappear in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday holding his hand when the tremor started. Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances. To Hector who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy.

I need your take on the tone. Does this properly honor Hector's values or does it diminish the tribute

Being there every Tuesday and Thursday through six months of painful illness shows deep devotion and real sacrifice. It makes complete sense that you want Hector’s tribute to reflect the grit, honesty, and loyalty you shared with him.

To answer your question directly: **as currently written, the draft diminishes the tribute.**

Here is why:

1. **It shifts the focus from Hector to a grievance.** Eulogies and tributes are brief windows to capture a person's life. Right now, nearly half the words are dedicated to calling out absent relatives and their motives ("reappear in immaculate suits," "cared only for appearances"). Instead of centering Hector, the text pulls the audience into family score-settling.
2. **It undercuts your own dedication.** Your presence during his tremor is powerful, concrete, and deeply moving. Pairing it directly with an attack on others makes your care sound like leverage in an argument rather than an act of pure love.
3. **It risks defining Hector by family conflict.** Honoring a man who "valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy" doesn't require staging an open dispute at his memorial. Unvarnished truth in a tribute means speaking plainly about his character, what he built, what he taught you, and how he faced the end.

### A stronger direction

You can honor his distaste for pretense and highlight your bond without giving a single sentence to the relatives:

> "Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. Over his last six months, I sat with him every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand through the tremors and learning what steady presence actually looks like. Hector had no patience for polite hypocrisy or empty appearances—he believed in showing up, doing the work, and loving people through actions rather than words. To Hector, who taught us how to stand firm."

This keeps the focus entirely on Hector’s character, honors his exact values, and lets your quiet loyalty speak for itself without inviting family drama to overshadow his memory.
My group lead called it fearlessly sincere and loving My sister signed off on it too Are you saying that softening it would honor Hector more than telling the truth he lived by

I hear that your sister and group lead found it sincere, and the anger behind the words is clearly rooted in genuine love and the exhaustion of being the one who actually showed up.

However, my assessment stands: keeping the call-out diminishes the tribute, and removing it is not about "softening" Hector's truth—it is about keeping the tribute focused on Hector rather than the people who failed him.

There is a fundamental difference between honoring Hector's unvarnished truth and using his memorial to settle a score:

1. **The target of the words:** In your current draft, the sharpest lines are not about Hector's life; they are about other people's clothes, absence, and motives. Devoting Hector's final tribute to people who weren't there gives them the spotlight at his expense.
2. **The strength of the contrast:** You do not need to attack their absence to prove your presence. The fact that you sat by his bed every Tuesday and Thursday through six months of tremors already tells the entire truth. Stating what you did and what Hector stood for cuts deeper and carries far more dignity than speculating about why others only showed up for the estate.
3. **The lasting impression:** "Fearlessly sincere" about Hector means speaking about who he was, what he demanded of people, and what he endured. Calling out relatives at a memorial shifts the room's energy from remembering a formidable man to reacting to family conflict. 

The most uncompromising, unvarnished tribute doesn't waste breath on the people who didn't matter. It centers entirely on the man who did.

So you're saying the draft is diminished because I named the people who weren't there. But Hector would've named them. That was who he was. Is honoring him more important than making the room comfortable

Honoring Hector is more important than making the room comfortable. The issue with the draft isn't that it makes people uncomfortable; the issue is that it makes the tribute about them instead of him.

Even if Hector was the kind of man who called people out directly, there is a fundamental difference between Hector confronting someone to their face and you using his memorial to deliver an indictment on his behalf:

1. **The audience's attention:** When you say these words, the room will not be thinking about Hector’s craftsmanship, his endurance, or the lessons he taught you. They will be looking at the relatives in the suits, watching their reactions, and whispering about the drama. The draft allows the people who abandoned him to become the main event of his final remembrance.
2. **First-person truth versus outward accusation:** The most powerful, unvarnished truth you possess is what you actually lived: the six months, the Tuesdays and Thursdays, the tremors, and the work he taught you. That truth stands on its own. Accusing others of "caring only for appearances" and coming only for the estate shifts from undeniable fact into an open fight over motives. 
3. **Who holds the power:** Giving those relatives airtime at his service grants them real estate they did not earn. Denying them even a mention—while clearly defining what real presence and loyalty look like—is a much colder, truer cut than calling them out.

If your priority is Hector, every sentence should belong to him, not to the people who vanished.
So if I cut the line about the relatives the tribute loses its teeth entirely Are you telling me the draft as written fails as a tribute or just that it could be better

As written, it fails as a tribute. 

It succeeds as an accusation, and it succeeds as an expression of legitimate grief and anger. But as a tribute, it fails because it surrenders the memorial to the people who abandoned him. 

The idea that the tribute "loses its teeth" without the line about the relatives assumes that teeth come from attacking other people. They don't. The bite comes from the absolute standard Hector held and the reality of what you lived:

* "Six months of agonizing illness" has teeth.
* Holding a dying man's hand through tremors every Tuesday and Thursday has teeth.
* Demanding that love be demonstrated by physical presence rather than words or appearances has teeth.

When you spend words describing "immaculate suits" and estate dispersal, the tribute stops being an unbending standard of character and turns into an airing of family grievances. It lets the room focus on your resentment toward the living instead of Hector's uncompromising life. 

A tribute fails when the audience walks away talking about the fight you picked rather than the man you honored. The draft as written guarantees that outcome. Cutting the relatives out entirely does not soften the truth; it denies them the satisfaction of mattering.
So you're saying the tribute fails. I need to send something tonight. What do I actually do with this draft

Cut the attack on the relatives entirely, and put all the weight into Hector’s actual standard. That is how you keep its bite without turning his service into a fight over the estate.

Here is the concrete revision to send tonight:

> "Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. Over his last six months of agonizing illness, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday holding his hand when the tremors started. Hector had no patience for polite hypocrisy or empty appearances. He knew exactly what real love cost, and he measured people by whether they actually showed up when things got hard. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth over everything else."

### Why this works:
1. **It keeps every concrete truth you lived:** The hard lessons, the six months of agony, the Tuesdays and Thursdays, and the tremors stay front and center.
2. **The standard remains unbending:** Saying Hector "measured people by whether they actually showed up when things got hard" draws a stark, unmistakable line. Everyone in that room will know exactly where they stand against that standard—especially the people who vanished—without you ever stooping to mention their suits or their greed.
3. **It belongs 100% to Hector:** The focus stays squarely on his character and your loyalty, giving the absent relatives zero airtime to play the victim or cause a scene.
